utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We commence this afternoon the Defence case. It was indicated on Friday there would be an opening address. Is that to be, Mr. Rodic, or Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon to my colleagues of the Prosecution. The Defence is opening its case today, presenting its case, and I would like to give the opening statement. The indictment of the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal, or the indictment of the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal, against General -- Colonel General Pavle Strugar charges him with violating the customs and laws of war through six counts of the indictment. Over a period of five months, the Prosecution presented its case, trying to prove that one man, General Pavle Strugar, is responsible for the events in and around Dubrovnik in the autumn of 1991. The Prosecutor of the International Tribunal attempted to present the events that are the focus of this trial outside of its historical, social, and military context in force at the time. The Prosecutor attempted to present these events outside of the framework of the time period and the space in which one state was being broken apart by a secessionist armed rebellion in the republics of Croatia and Slovenia in the period of 1990 to 1992, which actually represents the peak of the destructive relationship towards the state community of the Yugoslav communities in the twentieth century. The context of the events from 1991 is possible to be presented only by taking into account the history of the Yugoslav state, starting from its emergence in 1918, the events in World War II, followed by the period of Communism, until the illegal secession carried out contrary to the constitution of the SFRY. The Yugoslav state was created after World War I, in 1918, with the unification of two, up until then, independent states of Serbia and Montenegro and the territory of the former Austro-Hungarian monarchy, which was inhabited by southern Slav peoples: Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. The Yugoslav state was a unitary state, founded on the state concept of one nation, or one people, and three entities: Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. The state was divided into banovina, which did not represent a territorial division according to the ethnic principle, but were divided in accordance with the administrative principle. The kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, later the kingdom of Yugoslavia, from its very creation, was burdened by numerous antagonisms. These antagonisms were a consequence of various mutually exclusive state and national programmes of the Yugoslav peoples. The Croatian political elite felt that the Yugoslav state was a kind of transitional period in its process of state and national independence. The first attempt to create an independent Croatian state was made in 1941, under German sponsorship, with the forming of the Ustasha Independent State of Croatia. With the victory of the allies in World War II, a Yugoslav state was again created, according to the federative model, comprising six republics. The rule of communists was established in 1945, and it forcefully suppressed ethnic hatreds, myths, and stereotypes. The concept of brotherhood and unity represented a universal formula for the resolution of the national question in socialist Yugoslavia. However, the unresolved national question represents the key reason for the breakup of the second Yugoslav state covered Croatian separatism, which exists in various forms, and existed throughout the period of existence of the Yugoslav state, culminated in the illegal secession, contrary to the Yugoslav constitution. With the arrival of the Croatian Democratic Community to power in the spring of 1990, the last step was taken in the breakup of the SFRY. In preparation for secession from Yugoslavia, Tudjman's HDZ assessed that in order to achieve such a goal, a conflict with the Yugoslav national army was inevitable. That is why immediately upon the setting up of the authority of the HDZ, it decided and forcefully embarked on, number one, an enormous strengthening of the police forces; under two, forming, at the same time, party paramilitary formations, specifically the Croatian National Guard, as the corps of a future army; and under 3, weakening as much as possible the power of the units of the JNA, which was stationed in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. The decision by Franjo Tudjman, president of the Republic of Croatia, which was the strongest political party in power in Croatia, the Croatian National Guard's corps was officially promoted as a military formation at a rally held on the 28th of May, 1991, in Zagreb. At that point in time, Croatia had about 60.000 soldiers and conscripts under arms, as well as 30.000 police officers. Of course, these numbers indicate the preparations that were being carried out at the time in Croatia for an armed secession, because in accordance with the peacetime establishment, since the Croatian National Guard's corps is not a legal formation, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, in the period prior to that, had a much smaller number of police officers than these numbers, which went as high as 30.000 in 1991. However, prior to that, in the course of November 1990, the Presidency of the SFRY was informed about the considerable import of weapons and materiel from Hungary for the needs of the paramilitary formations in the Republic of Croatia. Because of that, on the 9th of January, 1991, the Presidency of the SFRY reached conclusions and issued an order on the disarming of all armed formations which were not part of the united armed forces of the SFRY or organs of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and whose organisation was not established and was not in accordance with federal regulations. The Presidency of the SFRY issued a deadline for the implementation of this order, which amounted to ten days. However, the Croatian leadership, after requesting an extension of this deadline by 48 hours, on the 21st of January, 1991, raised the combat readiness of the entire composition of the forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Croatian National Guard's corps. In view of such a response by the authorities of the Republic of Croatia, subsequent three orders of the Presidency of the SFRY on the disarming of paramilitary composition, or paramilitary forces, were not implemented. Contrary to that, the whole world saw the photograph of the strangling of a soldier in an armoured transporter on the 6th of May, 1991, in the situation when the command of the Military Naval District in Split was under blockade, and on that occasion, soldier Sasa Gesovski was killed while another soldier and officer were wounded. Since that time, until the 25th of July, 1991, there were 126 cases of violent acts against the staff and facilities of the JNA in Croatia. In that period, six members of the JNA were killed and 87 were wounded. This was followed by a blockade of the barracks throughout the entire territory of the Republic of Croatia, which was implemented by cutting off water, electricity, telephone lines, food supplies, with the assistance of paramilitary units, also all exits and entrances to the barracks were blocked. Also, during one of the numerous signed truces in the period from the 2nd to the 11th of September, 1991, 115 armed attacks were registered, resulting in 11 deaths and 40 injuries of members of the JNA. In such circumstances, following numerous violations of the truce and evasion by the Croatian side of obligations that it had signed on to on the demobilisation of the paramilitary formations, something that was witnessed by observers of the European Community and the European Commission, the headquarters of the Supreme Command reached a decision to use the activities of certain military units to exert pressure on the Republic of Croatia to deblock the garrisons and the barracks where JNA units were stationed in the territory of this republic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The military leadership quickly had to create and make operational the armed forces that would be carrying out the operations against the paramilitary formations, and also the task of the military leadership was to form the military territorial component which would control the rear of the fronts, ensure that life went on in one way or another in the territory which at the time was mostly inhabited by a hostile population, or on the territory from where the population had moved out or had fled, out of fear of the consequences of military operations. One of these temporary formations was the 2nd Operational Group, which was established towards the end of September 1991, headed by its then commander, General Jevrem Cokic. Numerous problems are linked to the establishment of this temporary military group. We had the opportunity of hearing about this during the Prosecution case, that in the mentioned period, the 2nd Operational Group changed three commanders within a short span of time. After General Cokic, after he was wounded, General Ruzinovski came to head the 2nd Operational Group. And then, on the 13th and 14th of October, Colonel General Pavle Strugar came to head the 2nd Operational Group. At that time he was the lieutenant colonel general. The establishment of the 2nd Operational Group did not mean that a command was to be established, first and foremost, and that then this command should go to a post that was assigned to it as a command post, to familiarise itself with its area of responsibility, and only then bring in and deploy units that were intended for it, which would have all been in keeping with military rules. What happened was the exact opposite of that. The units were already either in that area of responsibility or geared towards it or were supposed to appear there only after mobilisation and a march. The command of the 2nd Operational Group arrived only after the General Staff issued an order, and it was only the General Staff of the armed forces that all of a sudden informed them that certain units came under their command. All the orders issued by the personnel administration of the General Staff regulating appointments of officers within the 2nd Operational Group contained a clause stating that these appointments were temporary rather than for an indefinite period of time. So it is not being contested that the 2nd Operational Group was a completely new and temporary formation, or rather, part of the temporary composition of the armed forces of the SFRY. Within the group at that time were parts of the 37th Corps, headquartered in Uzice. This corps otherwise belongs to the 1st Military District. Then, within the 2nd Operational Group were parts of the 2nd Corps, headquartered in Titograd, now Podgorica. This corps belonged to the 3rd Military District, that was headquartered in Skopje, in Macedonia. Then the 9th Military Naval Sector, with its headquarters in Kumbor, which otherwise was an integral part of the forces of the Military Naval District, whose headquarters were Split. Then parts of the 4th Corps, with its headquarters in Sarajevo, a brigade was active from that corps and it became part of the 2nd Operational Group. And all together, it belonged to the 1st Military District, whose headquarters were in Belgrade. When all of this is taken into consideration, one thing is striking, and that is that only the forces of the 9th Military Naval Sector were within their original zone of responsibility and that all other units were brought in from their respective zones and deployed in a completely foreign zone of responsibility unknown to them. When speaking of the area of responsibility of the 2nd Operational Group, one has to bear in mind the fact that this is a very big territory, because the zone stretched through the territory of eastern Herzegovina to the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia, republics of the SFRY at that time; then Bosnia-Herzegovina and Montenegro. It included that border too. On the north and north-west, the area of responsibility of the 2nd Operational Group spread all the way to the Neretva River Valley, and on the west to the Adriatic Sea, including the hinterland and the islands in the broader area of Dubrovnik and the peninsula of Peljesac. When speaking of the composition of the 2nd Operational Group, it is important to point out that mobilisation was carried out as a military exercise, because the then state leadership had not declared a state of war. In such circumstances, mobilisation of units was almost entirely reduced to the principles of voluntariness, because when a state of war is not declared, it is not possible to apply strict legal rules, in case someone does not respond to a call-up for a military exercise, or rather, mobilisation. The level of training and mutual cohesion and solidarity of officers and soldiers, then officers amongst themselves and commands and units, was virtually non-existent, with all the negative implications entailed by such a situation in terms of the overall combat readiness of the units and the entire personnel. As I've already pointed out, these were units that were put together in haste, as were their commands. There was a lack of proper training, and they were never trained, never trained, for tasks that lay in store for them, particularly not in the territory where these operations would eventually take place. The officers that were assigned to the command of the 2nd Operational Group had never carried out such duties until then. These were officers from the chief inspectorate of the national defence in Belgrade, then the centre of higher military schools in Belgrade and the school of reserve officers from Bileca. And all of this took place only some ten days prior to the commencement of combat activities. All of this constituted a major problem. Over a short period of time, these people had to be re-channelled from duties that were based on command, staff, teaching, and inspection, to command and operative duties, without a single day of psychological and professional preparation and reorientation. Such a fluid situation and the fact that the newly established command of the 2nd Operational Group was not familiar with it at all beforehand led to very frequent changes within the internal organisation and establishment to re-subordinations and attachments that took place practically every day, and also units were taken out of the group almost on a daily basis as well. Finally, when bearing in mind the period that we discussed rather extensively here, that is, the period from the 1st of October until December 1991, the above-mentioned problems I referred to led to the fact that parts of the 2nd Operational Group did not carry out practically a single stage of any operation with the same personnel involved. When speaking of the role and task of the 2nd Operational Group, they can only be viewed in the context of the situation in the Neretva River Valley and the broader area of Dubrovnik, and the importance that this area had for the defence and preservation of the common state, and which was still considered to be a possible and realistically attainable goal by the then political and military authorities of Yugoslavia. The region of Dubrovnik, the town itself, including the surrounding area and its closer and farther approaches on both sides of the Adriatic highway, had a central position at the border between Montenegro and Bosnia-Herzegovina that were still in the SFRY and the Republic of Croatia, which in that year, 1991, had already taken the path of secession to a considerable extent. Control over that area was of vital geostrategic importance for yet another reason. This was an area, including the water body, through which routes led, both by land and sea, that were relevant for the relocation of the equipment, and particularly personnel, of the Military Naval District, primarily the navy, the equipment and units that were still deployed in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, to the only safe port and naval base in the Adriatic, and that was the Bay of Boka Kotorska and the Montenegrin coast. Therefore, it was of special importance to ensure that the paramilitary forces of Croatia do not use that area for their military needs. The Neretva River Valley divides the western and eastern part of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Herzegovina, and in the lower part of the Neretva River, there were very important military localities of the then JNA, notably, major military warehouses in Gabela and Dretelj, as well as Mostar airport, and the teaching centre in Capljina. Mostar at that time was the only air base in the territory of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina from where it was possible to give air support to the withdrawal of war technical equipment from the northern and central Adriatic to Boka Kotorska. All of these were reasons why the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, could not allow, under any circumstances, to have the Mostar airport and the Neretva River Valley get out of their control. Also, it is a well-known fact that the town of Dubrovnik and the broader area surrounding it was vacant from a military point of view. That is to say that not a single military unit had been based in it or in that area from the late 1960s. That is precisely what the government and Yugoslav People's Army had made possible in the late 1960s, with a view to the further development of Dubrovnik and the importance it had from the point of view of tourism, culture, and history. It is for that reason that precisely during those years, the Yugoslav People's Army relocated from Dubrovnik, its naval landing brigade of the military sector of Boka, and the brigade was relocated to Trebinje. Contrary to this kind of position taken by the state leadership and the Yugoslav People's Army, and of course their behaviour and practice, we see that Dubrovnik was once again armed. On the basis of available documents, which we have at our disposal, both the Defence and the Prosecution, it is possible to establish that already at the beginning of 1991, in the police administration of Dubrovnik, the number of reserve policemen was increased, a wartime organisation set up, and the reserve police force trained. And the police administration of Dubrovnik sent out regular reports about the situation in defence preparations to the sector for defence preparations within the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia. That means we are now speaking about the beginning of 1991. There are also documents in existence from which we can see that the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia issued orders to all police administration units to step up the reserve force of the Croatian National Guard's corps by 70 per cent members of the reserve police force and 70 per cent of the newly procured weapons for different purposes. And according to the documents, this meant infantry weapons, it meant weapons for anti-aircraft defence, anti-armour defence, and mines and explosives. Furthermore, at the process of wartime preparations on the territory of the Dubrovnik municipality was started very much before the actual war events took place - and I should especially like to stress before the preparations began on the part of the JNA for launching an operation on the Herzegovina-Dubrovnik battlefield - can be borne out from the documents of the supervision service and information service of the Republic of Croatia, the centre for Dubrovnik's information. And the Defence will, of course, during its defence case be presenting that document to the Honourable Trial Chamber. From this document, we can see that the work of this information centre and monitoring centre began on the 1st of May, 1991, and already up until that date, all reconnoitring stations and observation stations on the territory of the municipality had been put in place. The task was to monitor - that was the basic task, to monitor and control all movement on the part of the units of the Yugoslav People's Army in the area. From all this, we can see that it was a case of clear-cut preparation on the part of the Republic of Croatia for war against Yugoslavia in the territory of the city of Dubrovnik, that same city which, in the 1970s of -- in the '70s of the last century, in fact, became a protected area, a protected town by UNESCO as a cultural heritage of prime importance. One of the main tasks of this centre was to monitor and inform and alert the people of the JNA's movements, and a particularly prominent indicator of the militarisation of Dubrovnik, militarisation of Dubrovnik, I say, is linked to the presence and existence of the ZNG Brigade, whose headquarters was precisely in Dubrovnik, as well as its main force, deployed in the town. And in addition to those forces, in Dubrovnik we saw the paramilitary forces being based there and operative from there, and they were centred around the certain Crna Legija, or black legion, which originated from western Herzegovina. And this Trial Chamber has heard mention of that -- another paramilitary formation that we call the HOS, the HOS, which belonged to a political party in the Republic of Croatia. As a cultural and historical heritage site, Dubrovnik was used by the Croatian side and abused for political purposes through the media. By not accepting demobilisation, that is to say, by not accepting the status of an open town, without any military presence, Dubrovnik, in that year of 1991, found itself in the zone of combat operations, the goal of which was to regain control of the territory of southern Dalmatia, until the final political solution to the Yugoslav crisis was reached and to reach the sea and take control of the approaches to Dubrovnik, both those in its vicinity and those further afield as well. This objective and goal required, necessarily, a blockade of Dubrovnik, both from sea and from land, and in this instance, the town of Dubrovnik itself, in no plan of the 2nd Operational -- command of the 2nd Operational Group, or any command above and below that level, was ever the target of operations, nor the object of attack. However, the very fact that Dubrovnik had been militarised and that the military -- there was military presence in Dubrovnik and that the military presence acted from Dubrovnik, the Croatian forces attacked the JNA forces, who suffered casualties, and the JNA was the sole legitimate force on the territory of the SFRY at that time. Regardless of the number of casualties, this could have been sufficient reason to merit taking control of Dubrovnik and establishing full military control over it. However, in order to avoid all the consequences that an operation of this kind would imply - it would, first of all, mean large losses and destruction to the civilian population and the buildings and facilities - the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the SFRY and the command of the 2nd Operational Group never had as its goal the control of Dubrovnik and taking over of Dubrovnik. The maximum goal envisaged by the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, was to achieve the town's demilitarisation, and we were able to see this through the Prosecution case and the evidence provided, the numerous documents calling for normalisation of life in the town, to have life and work returned to normal in Dubrovnik. However, when that was not accepted, through the will of the Croatian authorities, the goal that was then set was Dubrovnik's blockade, a blockade from land and from sea. When we speak about the crux of the indictment and if we focus on the event of the 6th of December, 1991 as the focal point, then that event should be viewed within the context as we have presented it. We should particularly like to emphasise that not even then, on the 6th of December, 1991, justice had not been the case before either, the goal of a concrete military operation and all other military operations that took place was not to take control of Dubrovnik at all, nor to inflict any kind of intentional damage to the cultural and historical monuments, or indeed the population of the town of Dubrovnik. Having said that, the Defence will show through the defence case, by calling witnesses and presenting material evidence in the form of documents, prove the following: The Old Town, as a cultural, historic monument, protected by UNESCO, during the period that the operations took place on the Dubrovnik-Herzegovinian battlefront, was abused and used for military purposes, and all this was done in such a way that the paramilitary formations made use of the Old Town and its positions in its immediate vicinity for purposes of provocation and for opening fire and targeting the units of the Yugoslav People's Army who were found in the Dubrovnik blockade. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The provocations and firing from the Croatian forces' positions at Mount Srdj and at other positions were intensive and daily, and this fact will be proved during the defence case. Next, the Defence will move to prove that the signing of the agreement on a truce after the negotiations that took place with members of the Croatian government was supposed to take place on the 6th of December, at noon, 12.00, noon, as Admiral Jokic indeed informed the Superior Command of the 2nd Operational Group. Furthermore, the Defence will move to prove during its defence case and the presentation of evidence that the operation, or rather, the attack on Srdj and the elevation there, and the attack was launched by the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Trebinje Brigade on the 6th December, that that operation was a planned operation with the knowledge of and encouraged by the command of the 9th VPS, Military Naval Sector. Furthermore, the Defence will move to prove that in the preparations for that operation, it was agreed to have the support of the 3rd Motorised Brigade of the 5th Partisan Motorised Brigade, which at that time was commanded by Lieutenant Colonel Miroslav Jovanovic, and support of the cannon battery of the 130-millimetre calibre, which was stationed at the airport at Cilipi. Furthermore, the Defence will move to prove during the defence case that the command of the 2nd Operational Group was not informed about the military action of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade which was launched at Srdj on the 6th of December, 1991. Furthermore, the Defence will prove that on the 6th of December, 1991, during the attack on Srdj and during the duration of that military operation, up until the withdrawal of the units of the 3rd Battalion of the Trebinje Brigade to its initial positions, the command of the 9th VPS, Military Naval Sector, did not inform the command of the 2nd Operational Group at all about what was going on. Similarly, the Defence will prove that the commander of the 9th Military Naval Sector, Vice Admiral Miodrag Jokic, did not stop the attack of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade at Srdj, as he testified before this Honourable Trial Chamber. The Defence will also show that the JNA did not fire at the fire positions deployed in the town of Dubrovnik itself until there was counter-firing from those positions and until serious losses were inflicted on the combat groups of the 3rd Battalion, which during that military operation had reached the fortress at Mount Srdj. In its presentation of its case, the Defence will show that on the 6th of December, 1991, the Old Town was abused, as well as the immediate vicinity of the Old Town of Dubrovnik, through military operations from there against the forces of the JNA at Srdj, Zarkovica, and other locations where units of the JNA were situated. The Defence will show that those forces, operating from the Old Town or its immediate environs, inflicted heavy losses to units of the JNA at Srdj. The Defence will further show that on the 6th of December, 1991, there was direct communication between the commander of the 9th Military Naval Sector, Vice Admiral Vokic and the military leadership in relation to the attack on Srdj. The Defence also believe that the evidence that it plans to present will entirely illuminate the role of Vice Admiral Miodrag Jokic in relation to the events of the 6th of December, 1991 and the following days, as well as the fact that General Pavle Strugar was excluded from those events because there was direct communications and there were orders which the military leadership of the JNA issued to Vice Admiral Miodrag Jokic. These briefly delineated topics in our opening statement will be dealt with in the course of the presentation of our case. We will also be dealing about other significant circumstances. These -- or this evidence, overall, makes the Defence convinced that it will persuade this Honourable Trial Chamber that there is no responsibility on the part of General Pavle Strugar for the events that he is being charged with. Your Honours, I have now concluded my opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic -- Mr. Rodic, I beg your pardon. That's probably a good time, then, to have a break. We'll resume after the break with the commencement of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see the first witness is waiting. Good afternoon. Would you please take the affirmation card that is handed to you now and read the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you please introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber. Could we have your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I am Slobodan Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us the date of your birth and where you live.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 17th of May, 1952, in Dubrovnik, and I'm living in Herceg-Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what is your profession.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm an electronics professional. I have my own workshop where I carry out my trade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you ever convicted in a court of law?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you the following thing, since we are both speaking the same language, in order for what we are saying to be translated, could you please make a little pause after the question, before you start your answer, so that we do not overlap. Could you please tell us where you were living in 1991, where you lived and where you worked?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 I was living in Herceg-Novi, where I live today, and this is also where I have my TV repair business.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us: In late summer of 1991, what was the situation in Herceg-Novi, which is on the border of the Republic of Montenegro and the Republic of Croatia? So could you please tell us what the situation was in that bordering area.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The situation was beginning to become complicated. When Tudjman came to power in 1991, tension began to grow. I will give you one example. In 1991, in midsummer, for example, in July, I was going to Dubrovnik with my wife and two daughters, and halfway there, when we were passing through Konavle, I was stopped by two police officers. One of them stopped in front of my vehicle. He placed his leg or his foot on the hood of my car, and he pointed an automatic rifle at me and at the co-driver. The second police officer stood next to the door, and he told me to come out of the car and to open the trunk of the car, which is what I did. He took the rifle and rifled through the things that were in the trunk of the car and said that I could leave. That is just one example. I was told by my local citizens in Herceg-Novi that similar things were taking place quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was the situation like that only when you were going to Dubrovnik or did it happen in other places?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as it happens, I was born in Dubrovnik. Both of my daughters were born in Dubrovnik. So that we were living in Herceg-Novi would go to Dubrovnik once a month or maybe more often. So we felt Dubrovnik was almost the same as Herceg-Novi. After my hometown, Dubrovnik was the first closest town. There were also some other towns in Montenegro, Kotor or Podgorica, but we mostly had connections with Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In that period, in late summer 1991, in view of the events in the country, in Yugoslavia at the time, and the socio-political events, could you please tell us what was the mood of the Dubrovnik citizens in relation to the situation in the country.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Every day on the media we would hear that all the water was cut off and the electricity to all the barracks in Croatia, that they were surrounded by irregular forces, the so-called Zengas, ZNGs, the Croatian National Guard's corps, so that the Yugoslav army found itself, the Yugoslav People's Army found itself in quite a difficult situation. This reflected on all of us. We felt that tensions and fear were growing from day to day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you know who these armed formations were in the Republic of Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those forces, the Croatian National Guard corps, because Herceg-Novi borders on Dubrovnik -- I don't know the exact number of those forces, but I do know that quite a sizeable unit took up the border on the Croatian side, facing the Montenegrin side. So tensions increased each day, and then this culminated -- I don't exactly know what day this was, but I know that it was in December [as interpreted] when the Croatian army fired eight mortar and cannon shells to the -- into the village of Malta, that is, the village that is closest to Croatia, and I saw personally on two or three trees the scars from these shells that were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: For the record, I would just like to say that this -- in the transcript it says that this happened in December. Could you please tell us whether this was in December or in September when you're talking about this shelling, these mortar and cannon shells?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: These eight were the cause, not only that, but this happened slightly to the north, but more to the south, in Prevlaka.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the time frame. Which month was this? When did this happen? In which month? I heard you say September, but in the transcript it says December. So could we clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: How could it be December? That is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, then it's a mistake in the transcript. We're talking about September.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, September.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, possibly it could be October.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what were the legal armed formations in the SFRY at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The only legal military formations were the Yugoslav People's Army. All these other units were irregular units, because Croatia at the time was not an internationally recognised state.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1991, were you perhaps summoned or called up into the army? And if you were, how did this happen? In what way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, in August, I was summoned to an exercise which I think lasted for about ten days, and this was in Kamena, just above Herceg-Novi. And during those ten days, there was an incident in Herceg-Novi. I've forgotten exactly who was involved. It was a foreigner. I don't know from which country. And he tried to set off an explosive device, and probably planted somewhere on the beach or some other place. And in the Stjepo Sarena Street in Herceg-Novi, when his vehicle went over the waterworks grid, the vehicle shook and the wires on the device were tripped, so there was an explosion. So this was the first incident that took place in Herceg-Novi in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive -- were you ever called up to the reserve forces in that period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1991, approximately on September 21st, I was summoned to a military exercise, and I reported to Kamena, to the assembly point. I actually went there a month before that, in August, for an exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And after you were summoned to go in August, did you return home and then were called up again, or were you on the military exercise the whole time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was at the exercise for about ten days, and I returned home, and then around the 21st of September I again was called up for a military exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what your duties were when you were on military duty and which unit were you in?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm an electronics expert, and that is how I was recruited, to be a radio technician in the JNA. At the time, I was a member of the Territorial Defence of the Herceg-Novi municipality, and I was a mechanic, a radio mechanic, attached to the main radio station of the municipal Territorial Defence. We had a large radio station there in one vehicle. And we had several smaller mobile transmitter radio stations, and they were of the RUP-12 type.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us: This TO unit of yours from Herceg-Novi, was it part of a larger military formation that it belonged to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The Herceg-Novi Territorial Defence were part of the Kumbor Military Naval Sector. Ilija Martinovic was the TO commander, my TO commander, and the commander of the military naval sector was -- I think he was a captain of a military ship. His name was Krsto Djurovic. And unfortunately, in the first few days of the war, the helicopter that he was in crashed, and that is how he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And who succeeded Krsto Djurovic as commander of the naval military sector?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: He was succeeded by Miodrag Jokic. He was our commander after Djurovic was killed, until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me if your TO unit left the territory of Montenegro, and if it did, when did it do so, where, which direction did it go in?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The first mobilisation was at Kamena. This is a village which is about five kilometres from Herceg-Novi. From Kamena we moved to the Porobici village, and from that village, we moved to the Konjevici village, and from that village we crossed the border into Croatia, and our first landing point was the village of Mikulici, above Cavtat, in the Dubrovnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us if your unit took up any positions outside of the Mikulici village, in some other places?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Our unit of the Herceg-Novi TO was stationed in Mikulici for some seven, eight, to ten days. I don't know exactly the deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, the precise date is not important. Just the locations.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The location was around Mikulici. Our units were deployed around there. But we stayed there very briefly and then we moved to Grude. This is a larger village in the Dubrovnik municipality. We were billeted in a private house, and that's where the TO Herceg-Novi command was. Next to us was the army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how long were you in the Dubrovnik Herzegovina front?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I received my summons on the 21st of September. We were in Kamena, Porobici, Konjevici villages for about ten days. I cannot remember now the exact date when we crossed the border, because this was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you. I'm asking you for how long were you on the front? When did you return home?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I returned home in late November, or maybe even on the 1st or 2nd of December. But that was more or less the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you return your military equipment right away?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Because I was a driver of this vehicle with the radio station. I still had the vehicle. It was parked in front of my house until December, perhaps until late December.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us: While you were at the front with your unit, what were your specific tasks? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As a radio technician or mechanic, it was my duty to be near the main radio station at all times, the radio station of the Herceg-Novi TO. My other task was to supply all our radio stations out in the field with batteries and to repair them if there should be a malfunction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Before returning from the front line, as you said, at the end of November or beginning of December 1991, did you spend any other time at home? Did you spend any other day or two at home?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You were at the front line from September until the end of November or beginning of December. In that time period, did you perhaps stop by at home at some other time? Were you in Herceg-Novi?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I came home quite often. When I would take the used-up batteries from the field, then I would bring these batteries back to Kumbor, to the military barracks there. We'd have them recharged there, and then, on the following day, I would take a group of batteries, I would take these full batteries, take them out into the field, and that's what my daily work was like. I would take advantage of the situation. I'd stop by at home, take a shower, change.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: In your TO unit, in that period of time that we are discussing, were there any losses in terms of human lives?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The major losses, those that affected us, the people of Herceg-Novi, the most were incurred on the 8th of November, 1991. On that day, it was very peaceful. As a matter of fact, a few days before that, there were no actions whatsoever. And I asked the commander of the TO, Ilija Martinovic, to let me go home to get a bit of rest, to refresh myself. I arrived home around 5.00 in the afternoon, about 1700 hours, and just as I lay down to get some rest - I was still in uniform - a colleague of mine telephoned me, a colleague who came together with me, who was on leave as well. And he told me that men from our TO unit, the so-called Platoon of Specials, had some casualties at Bosanka. Some men were killed and others were wounded and that I should urgently go to the military hospital in Meljine it to see what we should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You go to the military hospital in Meljine then? And what did you hear there? What did you see there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I immediately went to the military hospital in Meljine. I went to the surgical ward, which is the ground floor, the right-hand side. I found a few of my comrades there who had been wounded. I talked to them for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Do you remember the names of these comrades?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Marko Poznanovic. He was wounded in the leg. Then Savo Gojkovic. He had a finger wounded, either on his right or left hand. Then there was Mandic. Mandic - I can't remember his first name right now - he was hit in the collarbone, and the bullet went into the body, down into the body. So it's the three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was anybody killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: They told me that our comrade from the unit, Dusko Pusic, was in the operating theatre right then, on the top floor of the surgical ward of Meljine hospital. I went upstairs and I waited in the waiting room to see what the outcome would be. A few minutes later, the surgeon walked out. His name is Bato Lakicevic. And I asked him, "Is Dusko alive?" He was silent. I asked him, "Is Dusko dead?" And he nodded, meaning yes. When I received this information, I went down to in front of the surgery ward and a group of people had already gathered by then, and they said that a dead man from the Yugoslav People's Army was supposed to be brought then, but we didn't know at that moment who this was. I turned around and I saw behind me the deputy commander of the TO, Djordje Radovic, and I said to him, "Djoko, let's go to Brgat to see what's going on with our men." However, tears streamed down his face and he said, "They are bringing my Baja now." That is his brother. Obren Radovic was his name; his nickname was Baja. He was in Niksic. He got killed as he was trying to pull men out from Bosanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: After the body of Obren Radovic was brought, did you stay in Meljine or did you go somewhere?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: How should I put this?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you could just try to be a bit more succinct.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Since there were vehicles of the TO from Herceg-Novi that were there with their tyres punctured, they asked me to take my own car to take Djordje Radovic, the uncle of the late Baja, to go to Niksic to tell his parents what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is that what you did?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I had no fuel, so that somebody else would do it instead of me, so that I could go to Brgat to see what happened to my comrades. However, they immediately brought two jerrycans of fuel. They filled up my car. And I had no choice but to get into my car and to travel via Risan and Grahovo, and during the night we arrived in Niksic. This was an exceptionally difficult night. I knocked at the door. The neighbours went out -- came out and the parents and Baja's grandfather. That is one of the hardest nights I ever had in my life when I told them what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, I will have to ask you to give shorter answers, more succinct answers. Time is precious to us. Tell me: After Niksic, where did you go and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: During the night, we got into another car, another car from Niksic joined us, and then, with two cars, we returned to the Meljine hospital. We arrived in Meljine, say, around 6.30 or 7.00. I brought them to the morgue. And when I took them into the morgue, I didn't even say goodbye to them. I just turned around and I ran to the gate of the Meljine hospital, in order to go to Brgat to see what had happened to our men.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What is the reason for that? Why did you go to Brgat? All the soldiers who were wounded, were they all taken out on that day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. On that day, they only brought the people that I mentioned: Those who were at the surgery ward on the ground floor of the hospital, and Dusko Pusic, who passed away in the operating theatre. Our other dead and wounded were at Bosanka. And Brgat is the closest feature to Bosanka, and that's why I wanted to go to Brgat as soon as possible, so that we would get organised and see how we can get them out, out of that difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. When you came to Brgat, what did you do in relation to this assistance that you rendered to your wounded comrades?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: When I came to Brgat, the situation was extremely difficult. People were very sad. There were even tears. And to tell you quite frankly, people were afraid too. I said, "Men, let's go." And I see nobody wanted to go. And then I said, "Give me the keys of the vehicle." And the captain of the TO from Herceg-Novi, Nikola Brajevic, threw me the keys of the TO vehicle that was a Niva, and I went from Brgat to Zarkovica and then along the asphalt road from Zarkovica to Bosanka. About halfway, I came across a JNA truck which bore the body of Bogdan Popovic. Slobodan Radovic, nicknamed Kruso, from Herceg-Novi was driving the vehicle, and Nesvet Gasal sat next to him. He was an employee of the Ministry of the Interior of Montenegro. For a while he was chief in Herceg-Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let's slow down, please. We don't need all these details. Can you just stick to absolutely essential matters. You said that on that truck was the body of the late Bogdan Popovic. Was he then transferred to Meljine too?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Bogdan Popovic was transferred on that truck to the hospital in Meljine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please: Was there anybody else who had stayed at the position, I mean the wounded persons, at this position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were some dead and wounded who were still at Bosanka. There were two groups there. There was one group of about eight men, if a squad is ten men. They were up towards the repeater at Srdj. And that's where Budo Zarubica was. He was wounded. Then another wounded person was Golub Mijovic. And together with them was a dead man, Vojica Pejovic. And also, Minjo Golub, another one of our soldiers who was a physical therapist by training, he got these two men out of a dangerous zone, a zone that was endangered by the Croatian fighters. He came and went twice, and then when he brought Pejovic he said he passed away. He can no longer be saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please: Why it was a problem to get these people out, the dead, the wounded? Why was it a problem to bring in the bodies?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Bosanka is actually a hunting area above Dubrovnik, and there are a lot of tangerine trees growing there, and it's a very difficult terrain to negotiate. It was very hard to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where were there any other dangers involved in relation to getting these men out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a road between Bosanka and Srdj, but we didn't dare use the road because we would have been hit by Croatian soldiers from the Srdj repeater, and also perhaps from Dubrovnik or Bosanka. It depended on the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: While these soldiers that you mentioned a few minutes ago were being taken out, were there any other casualties who -- among those who were trying to get the wounded and dead out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: When Bogdan Popovic was being taken out, Marko Komarica went to get him and Bajkovic, Obren Bajkovic. It's not Obren; I've forgotten his first name. We called him Baja, at any rate, and he came from Bar. So it was the two of them who lifted Vlado, but there was a rifle by Vlado's head, and Bajkovic told him to get the rifle. Komarica leaned over to fetch the rifle, and at that time a bullet came and killed him. He got into his head [as interpreted] and actually ruptured a blood vessel, which is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who was it who was doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the Croatian army from Bosanka. Bogdan Popovic and Vlado Zarubica, Bogdan was wounded lethally. They were both hit by Croatian troops from Bosanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me: Did you yourself take part in carrying some of these soldiers out, getting them out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As for Bogdan Popovic, I only came halfway, and we brought them to -- him to Brgat and sent him to the hospital in Meljine. Then when we sent Bogdan Popovic, then I started going towards Bosanka, but Gaso Mijatovic said to me, "Slobo, Savo Vidakovic is in the woods with a kombi van," and he brought him and Kruso to go looking for the two Pejovics by car for as long as you could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please tell me who is Gaso Mijatovic, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Gaso is a MUP employee who lives in Herceg-Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why did he go to Bosanka?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a personal friend of Vojica Pejovic, and he came to get him out of there. When he came to the area of Zarkovica, he went to the command at Zarkovica, to Colonel Garvo Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why? What was the reason he went to Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The reason was that he came to get Vojica out. And he went to see Gavro Kovacevic because he wanted him to explain the situation in the field to him so that he could try to get his friend out. Colonel Gavro Kovacevic said to him that in Bosanka there are over 70 armed soldiers. And he said to him: "See, I have a helmet on my head, and the situation is extremely difficult here. I'm exposed to mortar fire all the time. They are shooting at me from Dubrovnik. Even a mortar is targeting me. It is mounted on a vehicle." This mortar was targeting him from the Old Town and kept changing positions. So Gavro Kovacevic was in a rather difficult position. And when he finally asked him, when Gaso Mijatovic finally asked him, "Where is Vojica Pejovic, wounded or dead?" He just turned his back to him and Gaso said, "I was so taken aback that I simply walked out." And then he went to look for Vojica, and he came across the troops of Lieutenant Sikimic, with his soldiers. They found Bogdan Popovic, and they put him on a military truck. This military truck was taken over by Slobodan Radovic, Kruso, and Gaso Mijatovic. It was two sergeants from Herceg-Novi that took this truck and, as I said, they brought it to Brgat and from there they went to Meljine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. What you've just told us linked to Colonel Gavro Kovacevic at Zarkovica, how do you know about all that? Did you personally talk to anybody or did you receive the information from anybody?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: When I went to Zarkovica for the second time and Bosanka, Gaso Mijatovic did not allow me to go alone. He went -- got into the jeep, the Niva jeep with me, and when we reached Zarkovica, we went on foot to lock for Savo Vidakovic's van, and on the way there I asked Gaso, "How come you're on the battlefield?" Because he was a MUP employee and he shouldn't have been there in the first place, establishment-wise. So he came privately to try and save --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, would you please listen to my questions and try and give us as succinct answers as possible. And I had a very short question for you. A moment ago, you told us something and you mentioned that Colonel Kovacevic explained something, that he said that there were over 70 Croatian soldiers at Bosanka, for example, and that he was exposed to fire from -- mortar fire from Zarkovica, that he was being targeted, and that he was being targeted with a mortar and a mobile truck from the Old Town. So my question to you was: How come you know that? Did somebody tell you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Gaso Mijetovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, please, but once again, briefly: Did you take part, and if so, how did you manage to pull out Vojica Pejovic when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Gaso and myself tried together with Lieutenant Sikimic's soldiers to do that. After now, we realised that we didn't know the terrain at all. It was getting dark and we didn't know what to do and couldn't proceed in that fashion. So we decided to get a military transporter and to try and do it that way. So we went back to Brgat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, was the reason -- you were looking for a transporter, you say. Was the reason because you were being targeted at, fired at?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They were firing at us from Dubrovnik non-stop. And when I was in the Niva jeep going to Bosanka, where we -- where I met Kruso and Gaso carrying the body of Bogdan, higher up above me there were bullets flying by. So I had to extinguish my lights. Had I had my lights on, it would have been the end of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. And as you weren't able to pull your fellow comrade's body out, you mentioned a transporter. What did you actually do with that transporter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: We went to Brgat and our TO commander, Martinovic, and Gaso Mijatovic, they went to a house across the road where Lieutenant Colonel Licanin [phoen] was, he was a signalsman, and he called Admiral Jokic to provide him with a transporter. Jokic said there was no transporter at Kumbor and that the naval military district did not have one, did not possess a transporter. Somebody then said there was a transporter to be had in Trebinje. So I went off in the 128 vehicle belonging to the TO of Herceg-Novi, with three of my colleagues. We went to Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, in Trebinje, in the barracks or wherever --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. To the Trebinje barracks, which is where my friend Zdravko Radakovic was. I don't know how, but he managed to find an army transporter, and he said, "It's coming very quickly and will arrive there when you arrive." And that's what happened. The transporter got to Brgat very quickly, and Colonel Jovanovic and seven or eight of us got into the transporter and we reached Zarkovica, and Colonel Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me who Colonel Jovanovic is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Jovanovic, we called him Kurd, and he came from Serbia, from somewhere in Serbia. At least that's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether you managed to use the transporter to pull out the body of the late Pejovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: We managed to get through as far as we were able to go and then Gaso Mijatovic and Gojko Pejovic, who worked in the MUP, both of them, they managed to establish connection via a radio station, and they called the station up, or rather Colonel Jovanovic called him and I listened in to the conversation, where Gojko Pejovic, he was in a forest with Budo Zaropovic [phoen] who was wounded and Govo Mijovic, and another reconnaissance man from Kotor and he was very cold-blooded and said, "Don't try and get through to us from Bosanka because Bosanka is full of Croatian soldiers. You won't have any chance of doing that. But come in the morning and take the opposite side, take the northerly route and try and pull us out that way."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now tell us how long this operation of pulling them out lasted.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at about 1.00, 2.00, we returned to Brgat and the transporter went back to Trebinje. At dawn the next morning, we were supposed to pull the people out. However, the transporter did not return, as they had promised to do. So we had to organise two routes, took two paths. One group went to try and pull out the wounded, that is to say, Budo Mijovic and Gojko Pejovic and Milic, and I went back to Trebinje to fetch the transporter. We returned one or two hours later, and nine of us got into the transporter and we reached Zarkovica. From Zarkovica, we went down to Bosanka, because at that point in time, Bosanka actually fell and we were informed of this by captain of the warship Zec. Anyway, they informed us that Bosanka was free.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what date that was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were killed on the 8th, so that was the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: When did that operation of pulling out the bodies end?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, we did our best. We went towards Srdj. We took the forest route.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, I have to interrupt you to tell you that time is very precious, so please don't go into the details. Just give me brief answers to my questions. And my question was: Do you remember whether the pulling-out operation of the two men ended?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, that same day, we reached Vojica Pejovic that day. He was dead. We picked him up and tried to carry him. But the team of men weren't able to finish the job. So we had to cover the body with blankets and we hid him in a bush. And the next day, in the morning, we organised another team of men to go out and try and collect up the body. And we succeeded the next day. We pulled the body out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: From that first day, and you said it was the 8th of November, I believe, when you learnt about the death and wounding of your colleagues, how many days went by until you were able to finish the operation and pull out the bodies, the bodies of the killed and the wounded?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That all went up to the 11th. On the 10th, we had the well-known event that took place in Herceg-Novi, in Kumbor, in front of the military barracks there. There were demonstrations that were held on the part of dissatisfied Herceg-Novi inhabitants and their families. They all rallied there in front of the barracks and were critical of why things were progressing so slowly and in such an unorganised fashion, as they said, why everything was going so slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you yourself present there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I just heard this from some of my friends because the previous days I was at Bosanka and I was busy pulling out the dead and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about some of the men from your unit? Did they take part in those protests?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say. I can't remember. I don't know. All I do know is that it took place, but who was there, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please: You mentioned the name Komarica, the name of a soldier called Komarica who assisted in the operation of pulling out the wounded fighters from your unit. Could you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: His name is Marko Komarica and he was a soldier of the well-known 3rd Battalion. He was a young guy of 18 at the time. And during the pulling out operation of Vlado Zarubica when nobody dared to pull him out, many refused to do so, didn't follow orders, he took it upon himself to do that and he demonstrated great courage in pulling the body of Vlado Zarubica out. And he became very popular in Herceg-Novi and that's how I came to meet him in the first place. And until the end of his military service, we were on very good terms and good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the 3rd Battalion. Which 3rd Battalion do you mean? You said that Komarica was a member of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a soldier in the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, but what 3rd Battalion? Who commanded the battalion? Do you know under whose command Komarica was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The commanding officer was Vladimir Kovacevic, nicknamed Rambo. He was Komarica's commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: After these events and after the operation of pulling out the killed and wounded, did you see Komarica after that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw Komarica several times after this operation, and after that courageous act on his part. I visited him several times. He was up at Bosanka. That's where his unit was stationed. So I went to see him several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me this now, please: Where were you exactly on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, 1991, I was already at home, but I hadn't returned the jeep that I had been issued, nor my personal weapons. So on that day, I listened to the Herceg-Novi news at 3.00 p.m. and heard Radio Herceg-Novi which broadcast that there was a battle at Srdj by Dubrovnik on that day and that there were two men killed. And as soon as I heard that, I got into the jeep and drove as fast as I could to Brgat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I do apologise for interrupting you, but listen to my question, please. Tell me why you, who were in Herceg-Novi, when you heard the news, why you set out for Brgat. What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my unit had withdrawn several days prior to that from that area, but I had a lot of colleagues there, Komarica being one of them, this 18-year-old man Komarica, who was so brave. So I went mostly for his sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you worried about him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was worried about him. I was anxious. And when I drove the jeep along the Cavtat road, where you come to the hairpin bends and the canyon, you could see the repeater at Srdj very well, and I noticed that every two or three minutes a shell would fall on Srdj, and there was a strong wind blowing on that day and I could see the wind blowing around the smoke from the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me ask the questions, please. And my next question is this: So this was on the road, you say, to Brgat. Now, on the way, when you reached Brgat, did you stay there for any length of time? Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I went via Brgat and Zarkovica and reached Bosanka. When I reached Bosanka, I noticed a house which was still under construction. And I noticed several soldiers standing round that house. I parked the jeep, got out, and went inside, into the house. The house was full of our soldiers, and among those soldiers I think there was frigate captain Jovo Drla [phoen]. I think that was his rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what was he doing there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a very difficult situation there because the army, the soldiers, were angry and nervous after five of their comrades had been killed, and Jovo was in charge of conveying to them orders from the command that they had to relinquish an attack on Srdj, the attack on Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I apologise for that. Tell me now, please. You say that Jovo Drlan [phoen] explained to the soldiers that the command did not allow them to march on Srdj. What was the soldiers' reaction to those words of his?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers reacted by swearing. They used derogatory language to speak about Zec and Jokic. And when I heard this swearing going on, as I wasn't interested, I left the house and asked the soldiers standing outside where Marko Komarica was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I interrupt. There is a name missing. Zec and name missing. Perhaps if the witness can repeat. Page 40, line 16: "The soldiers reacted by swearing. They used derogatory language to speak about Zec and," somebody else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As we're correcting the transcript, there was something else that wasn't introduced into the transcript. So would you repeat. On the 6th of December, how did it come about that you drove off to Bosanka? What happened? What happened to make you set out for Bosanka?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I listened to Radio Herceg-Novi and heard that there had been military -- a military confrontation at Bosanka and that there were two men killed. That's what Radio Herceg-Novi broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell us when that was.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That was on the 6th of December, exactly at 1500 hours over Herceg-Novi Radio, the news bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translations continues]... interrupt. I think the witness had already responded and his previous comment was that there was a battle on Srdj, but my learned friend asked the question again and got -- led the witness to say Bosanka. I think this is very inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I was misunderstood but it doesn't matter. We're not challenging that there was fighting at Srdj. What I asked the witness was what the reason was that he set out from Herceg-Novi towards Bosanka. Because it wasn't recorded in the LiveNote that he had listened to the news bulletin at 1500 hours, during which he heard that two soldiers were killed at the fighting at Srdj, in the fighting at Srdj. So I wasn't leading the witness towards Bosanka. He set out towards Bosanka, because there wasn't fighting at Bosanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, did you -- after what you have described to us, hearing and seeing at Bosanka, did you afterwards learn where Marko Komarica was, the soldier Marko Komarica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: They told me that the killed and the wounded were in Trebinje. I got into my vehicle and went to Trebinje. In Trebinje, I went to the military medical centre or hospital - I don't know what it's called - and I asked them where the mortuary was. I went there, and I saw five people who were killed on that day at the Srdj repeater. And they are Mesaros, Divjan, Tasovac and two other people whose names I've forgotten because it was many years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. At the hospital in Trebinje, did you find Marko Komarica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Marko Komarica, I was told there at the hospital that he was wounded lightly and that he was transferred to the Meljine hospital. So I got into my car and went to Meljine. In Meljine --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us: Did you find Marko Komarica in the Meljine hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I found him in the military hospital in Meljine, with his friends, Svetislav Rakovic and Bodiroga - I don't know his name - from Trebinje. All three of them were wounded. Bodiroga was injured in the spine because he was carrying Mesaros's dead body from Srdj. Marko Komarica had a face wound. Rakovic was also wounded, but I don't remember where.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please just answer briefly. These wounds of Komarica and Rakovic, were they serious?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. These were light wounds, light facial wounds. I took them to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did Komarica and Rakovic, were they supposed to stay in the hospital or were they supposed to go back to their units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: They were lightly wounded, and they were supposed to perhaps spend the night in the hospital and return to the unit in the morning. And Bodiroga was supposed to stay there for a couple of days. So I took the two of them back to my house so that they could spend the night there, and then -- so that I could take them to Brgat the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you took the soldiers Komarica and Rakovic to your house on the 6th of December, did you talk with them about their operation in Srdj, what happened, how it happened? Did you hear from them what happened, how they were wounded and did you hear anything about the operation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we got to my house, I asked them what happened, and they told me, Komarica and Rakovic, that on the 5th of December, they were assembled somewhere - I don't know where - and that the warship captain Zec asked them who was brave enough to get those grannies out of Srdj. There was a silence, and after a few seconds, Bodiroga put his hand up first and he said, "I will do it."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about Bodiroga who was in the Meljine military hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the Bodiroga who was wounded when he was bringing out -- he was the one who carried Mesaros most of the way from of Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. And did anybody else volunteer except for Bodiroga?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Komarica, Marko volunteered and Svetislav Rakovic, Mesaros also volunteered and a few other men whom I never saw before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And did they tell you anything else about that 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: They told me that on the 5th of December, they agreed that there would be an attack early on the 6th on the Srdj repeater. They were promised safety vests and shock bombs. They didn't receive the flak jackets, but only the shock bombs, which were taken by the platoon or unit commander Bodiroga.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During the Srdj operation, did anybody from that group that included Rakovic and Komarica get killed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They went to attack Srdj early in the morning, and there was one person who was killed first, Mesaros. He was a private first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was he a regular private?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. And when they came to my house after staying at the Meljine hospital, they said that it was Mesaros's and mine last day of military duty. Had Mesaros survived that day, the next day he was due for a discharge so that he could return home back to his parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they tell you anything about how the operation on Srdj proceeded?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They told me that when they arrived almost to the top of the Srdj repeater, they were fired at from Dubrovnik, from mortars. There was fierce mortar fire and they had casualties. There were five of their comrades who succumbed. Komarica Marko was lucky. Rakovic told me that wherever Komarica was, five seconds after that a shell would drop there. But he was lucky and each time he managed to escape, and he ended up with just superficial scratches.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did Komarica and Rakovic perhaps tell you how long they were at Srdj and what happened as long as they were there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: They were on Srdj during that day. It's December; the days were short. So when I came -- I left Herceg-Novi at 3.00, so I got there at 3.40 p.m. it was already all over. We didn't go into too many details, but they had already returned from Srdj earlier. The wounded and the dead were taken to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Because you went to Bosanka yourself on the 6th, did you see Srdj? Did you see if there were any JNA soldiers at Srdj at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: When I got there, there were no soldiers at Srdj. The soldiers were at Bosanka, in a house which was still being built. It wasn't completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Jovan -- did Komarica tell you where he withdrew to from Srdj?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: They pulled back around that house somewhere and that's where the sanitation took care of them and took them to the various hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Komarica and Rakovic spent the night between the 6th and the 7th at your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
