utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And then on the 7th of December, did you drive them and go with them to the unit or did they return by themselves?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I put them in my car and took them to Brgat, to their commander, Vladimir Kovacevic, called Rambo, and they asked him to let them go to the funeral of their friend, Mesaros. When we came into the hall of the command where Rambo was, I came close to the door and I heard the warship captain Zec tell Rambo Kovacevic, "Young man, now you will go for a longer holiday." Then we waited for a while and then Rakovic and Komarica went in to see Rambo Kovacevic so that he would give them permission to go to Subotica. He made that possible for them. And while I was waiting for them in the hall, in the corridor, I went outside for a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you for a bit. You said that you heard someone saying, "Young man, you are going to go on a longer holiday." Could you please tell us who that was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was Admiral Zec. We were good friends. I knew him well, so I could recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was his rank?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time he was a warship captain. Later he became an admiral.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How did you know that it was war captain Zec who was saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Because I spoke to him several times and I know his voice very well, and I'm sure that it was he who told Rambo Kovacevic, "Young man, you will be going on a longer holiday."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you enter the office?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was standing in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Just take it easy, please. How do you know whose office it was from where you heard that voice?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was brought there by Rakovic and Komarica to that door because that was the door of the office of their commander, Vladimir Kovacevic. So it was logical for him to be saying that to Vladimir Kovacevic, especially because it was known that there was some problem there, because I could see reservists from Trebinje or from someone in Herzegovina who were standing around the building and from the conversation with them. I could hear that they had heard that the army wanted to replace Rambo Kovacevic and they were not allowing that to happen. So they prevented him from being replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you talk with these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I just spoke with them informally, and I could see that they were resolute in their support for their Captain Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did they explain why?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's known what happened that day, and they were standing by their captain, the unit commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What were the soldiers saying? What were they explaining?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: They said that they knew that there was an operation to attack Srdj and then another order came later, that this operation should be stopped. So soldiers, as soldiers are, were unhappy because things were being done this way and because they wanted to replace a person who was not to blame for anything. He was just trying to protect his soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Did Komarica and Rakovic get permission from their commander to be absent from the unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Within a minute or two, he signed their permits for them. I put them in my car, took them to the bus station in Herceg-Novi, saw them off to the bus for Subotica, because they were going to the funeral of their comrade Mesaros.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my examination-in-chief. Thank you very much. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Ms. Mahindaratne will conduct the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Novakovic. My name is Ms. Mahindaratne and I will ask you questions on behalf of the Prosecution. So what's your ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were mobilised around 20th of September, 1991. That is correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you mobilised to participate in the Dubrovnik operation? Were you informed that you would be mobilised to participate in the Dubrovnik operation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was just called up for a military exercise, which started in Kamena. This is a village which is five kilometres from Herceg-Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, at the stage you were mobilised, what military training had you received in terms of weapons training or duration of your training? Just a brief response would do.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was called up into the reserves several times for exercises. This one lasted a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you had any form of training in weapons at that stage, or was your task going to be mainly with regard to operation of radios?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: My main task was to take care of the radio communications, and I was also familiar with personal weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In September 1991, you said that your Territorial Defence unit of Herceg-Novi was subordinated to higher command. What was the name of that command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The higher command was called Military Naval Sector of Kumbor. I perhaps did not give you the correct name, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And where were you based once you were deployed to participate in the Dubrovnik operation? Where was your unit based, the Territorial Defence unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: First we were summoned for a military exercise and not for an attack on Dubrovnik. We went to Kamena. This was approximately on 21st of September. We spent about seven or eight days in Kamena and then we --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... interrupt you, Mr. Novakovic. If you could just respond. Once you were deployed to participate in the Dubrovnik operation, where were you based? You don't have to go to the time before that. Once you were deployed towards the attack, where were you based? Where was your unit based?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: First we came to the village of Mikulici. We spent a couple of days there. From Mikulici we were transferred to Grude, and that is where our unit was stationed for a while. That was the TO unit from Herceg-Novi. That's where the command was. I was always with the command because that's where the radio station was. I had to be on standby in case of a malfunction or something, so that I could fix it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So your assignment or your base was at Grude right through the time you were deployed in the Dubrovnik operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How far is Grude from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Grude is halfway between Herceg-Novi and Dubrovnik, about 20 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And how far is Grude from Brgat?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It's about 22 to 23 kilometres from Brgat.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So how is it that you seem to have been present at Brgat constantly, despite the fact that your base, your duty station, was Grude?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The witness did not say at any point that he was stationed at Brgat all the time. Could my learned friend please pay attention to what has been said so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question was not that he was stationed at Brgat. My question was:

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How is it that you seem to have present in Brgat constantly when your duty station was -- Grude, Grude. Perhaps my learned friend should pay attention to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Petrovic. Do you have an answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have an answer. My task, as the radio mechanic, was to supply the radio stations out in the field with charged batteries. One of the radio stations was with the special unit that happened to be stationed at Brgat. So I went every day or every other day, depending on when they called me, when they used up their batteries, so that I could take the spent batteries and give them a charged one. So that is how I happened to see them every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What was this place or command or unit in Brgat that kept calling you to replace their batteries? What was at Brgat?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a unit of the TO of Herceg-Novi. I belonged to this Territorial Defence of Herceg-Novi. This was a platoon of this unit of ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you also aware that the command post of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade was also in Brgat?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you went to the post of Herceg-Novi Territorial Defence unit that was in Brgat, were you aware that there were other command posts or other military installations of the JNA in Brgat?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assumed that there were others, but I did not know about anybody else. I only knew about my own unit. My only duty was to charge and replace the batteries of my TO unit from Herceg-Novi, but I did not know otherwise who belonged to which unit. I just knew about this Komarica, who was a friend of mine, that he belonged to Rambo's unit. As for the rest, I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you know that Rambo, or Captain Vladimir Kovacevic, was the commander of the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not hear this properly. Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know that Captain Vladimir Kovacevic, or Rambo, was the commander of the 3rd Motorised Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I knew. Perhaps not at the very outset, but later on, when I spoke to Komarica, I found out that he was a soldier of that 3rd Battalion and that his commander was Vladimir Kovacevic, nicknamed Rambo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And your friend Komarica belonged to the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So did you not visit him at his base when you visited Brgat?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was, as I said, out there to visit for a few times. Whenever I'd go to Brgat, I'd always take advantage of that and go and see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And so as such, you do know that a unit of the 3rd Battalion was in fact based in Brgat, contrary to what you said earlier on? You said that you did not know that the command post of the 3rd Battalion was in Brgat. But you visited your friend at his post in Brgat?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Things are a bit more complicated than what you said. His command was probably at Brgat, but he was at Bosanka, halfway from Bosanka to Srdj, underneath a wall. That's where his little tent was, an improvised tent, and that is where he was on guard duty. I did not ask him, "Where is your command," or whatever. I was not interested in that. I was just interested in whether he was alive and well, whether he was healthy, how he was doing. I never asked him about his command or his commander or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you did not know where his command post was at all?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I had no idea where his command was. Only on the day when I brought them so that they could go to Subotica, it's only then that I found out that that was the command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, what was the name of your unit commander, the territorial unit -- Territorial Defence unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Territorial Defence of Herceg-Novi was Ilija Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you were directly subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was he a good commander in that did he have command and control over his subordinate units in that did you and your colleagues comply with the orders issued by him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I follow the orders issued by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And he, in turn -- did he seem to -- did he comply with the orders issued by his higher command? Were there any allegations that he did not comply with orders?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I, as a plain soldier, did not know who issued orders to him or whether he was carrying them out. I just knew that I was carrying out the orders that he issued to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you testified in examination-in-chief that when there was a move to replace Captain Kovacevic, his subordinate soldiers stood by him and insisted that he should not be removed. Did you ever learn, perhaps from your friend Komarica, that Captain Kovacevic had control over his subordinate units and that they in fact complied with the orders issued by Captain Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew from Komarica and from the others there that Rambo Kovacevic was in total control of the situation in his unit. In his unit, he was an exceptionally good officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And is there anything that was perhaps repeated to you by your friend Komarica or anyone else which would give one to draw the conclusion that Captain Kovacevic may act in contravention of his superior orders, that he may not comply with orders issued from his higher command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when talking to Komarica and others, I could not understand in any way that Kovacevic was not carrying out the orders issued by his command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said you were -- your Territorial Defence unit was subordinated to the 9th Naval Sector. Were you ever made aware when you and your unit was being deployed in the Dubrovnik operation that your unit was being attached to a specially established or specially created command, namely, the 2nd Operational Group, which had been assigned to carry out the Dubrovnik operation? Were you made aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. I thought, and knew, that I was only subordinated to Ilija Martinovic, commander of the TO of Herceg-Novi and that we were within the military naval sector of Kumbor, it was called Boka. I didn't know anything else. I just knew that we had an army commander. I don't know who it was exactly who was in Belgrade. I can't remember. A general, most probably. I can't remember his name now. But that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you heard of the term "2nd Operational Group" before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you heard of General Strugar, General Pavle Strugar, the accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I first heard of General Strugar and heard of him when I was a member of the Municipal Assembly of Herceg-Novi. When our army withdrew to the borders, then we had an extraordinary meeting of the Municipal Assembly of Herceg-Novi, and General Pavle Strugar took part in this meeting. I did not meet him personally then, but that's when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know that General Strugar was in fact the former commander of the Territorial Defence of Herceg-Novi? Did you know that -- I beg your pardon. Of Montenegro. Did you know that? You were yourself in the Territorial Defence, so did you know that your commander, commander of the Territorial Defence in Montenegro, was General Pavle Strugar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So it is your position that you did not know that General Strugar was in any way involved in the Dubrovnik operation? That is what you're saying today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I never saw him at the Dubrovnik theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question was not whether you had seen him, but did you know that General Strugar commanded the Dubrovnik operation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know that. I thought that the Dubrovnik operation was led by Krsto Djurovic until he got killed and from then on Miodrag Jokic. I had never heard of Strugar. I first saw him in Herceg-Novi. I actually thought that Rambo Kovacevic and his unit were all within the navy in Boka.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you made aware of the fact that one of the objectives of the war you fought in was to maintain a naval and land blockade around Dubrovnik? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not very well versed in that. I'm just an ordinary soldier. But what I roughly knew was that our objective was never to attack Dubrovnik. Had that been our objective, we could have shelled it every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I shall be grateful if you would confine your response to my question. Now, judging by what you said, your understanding was that the naval activities around Dubrovnik were being conducted by the 9th Naval Sector and that you were not aware that the 2nd Operational Group command had any role to play in those activities? Is that a correct assumption?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I certainly did not know about that. Now, whether that is right or not, you can be the judge of that. But I had no idea that we were subordinated to anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about -- I beg your pardon. You talked about attending a municipal meetings, Municipal Assembly meetings. Were you a member of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the Municipal Assembly in 1991 and 1992, something like that, maybe even 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what political party were you affiliated with?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I belonged to the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, which precisely in that period, between 1991 and 1992, was turned into the Democratic Party of Socialists of Montenegro. But I never became a member of that party. I was only a member of the Municipal Assembly. I completed my term of office. But I remained a member of the League of Communists and I did not take a party membership card of the democratic party of socialists of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is a party known as SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. That is the Democratic Party of Socialists. Its president used to be Momir Bulatovic, and now its president in Milo Djukanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any relationship to Mr. Predrag Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I personally know Predrag Bulatovic, but I was speaking about Momir Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I know what you were speaking about. So my question to you was, the vice-president of Mr. Momir Bulatovic, the president of Montenegro, the vice-president, Predrag Bulatovic, was he in any way related to you? I'm asking about relationship. Aren't you his nephew or don't you have a close relationship to him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Predrag Bulatovic and I are not related at all. Since I'm a member of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, my party was in a coalition with his party, so we just know each other from these inter-party contacts, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, were you -- when you -- your -- the learned Defence counsel asked you as to whether you had any convictions; you responded in the negative. Were you not charged with the murder of a woman sometime in 1992 or 1991, or even perhaps later on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you where the confusion lies. The nephew of Predrag Bulatovic has the same name and surname as I do, Slobodan Novakovic. I've never seen him in my life and we are not related. And I found out this by accident by Nenad Vulevic, who happened to serve a prison sentence together with him in Spuz. So I did not have a criminal record at all, and I have never seen this Slobodan Novakovic ever in my life. I just heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You said you do not have a criminal record at all, but were you not charged for larceny in the lower courts of Herceg-Novi, a crime, an offence committed while you were a member of the Territorial Defence unit of Herceg-Novi? Were you not charged with larceny, the offence of committing larceny?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. In Tivat, I was asked to appear before a court of law. A reservist - I cannot remember his name right now - was charged with something, and he asked me to testify to the effect that I saw that he did not take part in any thefts. So that is what I did. I went there and testified that he did not take part in any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, just before the break, I asked you a question as to whether you were charged for the offence of aggravated larceny before the Herceg-Novi lower court, and you said no. Now, I put it to you that you were in fact charged for committing the offence of aggravated larceny and you were charged on 12 February 1992. Is that correct, or is that wrong? How do you respond to it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It's wrong, because, as I said, I was a witness. I testified for a reservist soldier. I think his name Zika Milosavljevic, who was accused and charged with some things, and they called me in to testify and I testified at the court in Tivat, not Herceg-Novi, but the military court in Tivat, where I gave a statement and said that I did not see Milosavljevic engaged in any looting or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. We move on. Now, your main task was to attend to the radio communication that was taking place around Dubrovnik with regard to the Dubrovnik operation. What was the state of the radio system or the communication system of the JNA forces at that time? Was there an efficient system? Was it in good working order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, during that time, it was efficient, quite efficient. We worked in the TO of Herceg-Novi and we were able to communicate with all our units. So that was within my area of expertise. Now, what they did in other units, I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in examination-in-chief, you said that your base in Grude was next to an army command. Which army command were you referring to? Was it the army command of the 3rd Battalion or -- I beg your pardon. Which army command were you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the command of the military naval sector, and that's where the commander of that unit was, if that's what he was. He had a rank at the time. I think he was captain first class. And his name was or is -- and he's here together with me just now in The Hague. We're in the same hotel. His name is Gojko Djurasic. And at the time, Gojko Djurasic was there, yes, that was the name, and I think that he held the rank of captain first class at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And so being based just next to where Captain Djurasic was during the time, you got to know him very well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was next to us, but we were the TO of Herceg-Novi, and I just happened to know the man personally, because as a mechanic I went to see to his TV set. There was something wrong with it. So I went to his house. So that's how I knew him. He was up at the battlefield. He had his command, I had mine, so we didn't have any points in common up at the front at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your testimony was that you went back home, you returned to Herceg-Novi, on -- at least late November or early December. You said 2nd or 3rd. So which means you were certainly not privy to what happened on the 6th of December morning in and around Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you heard about what was going on only through the radio?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. I heard it over the radio. And at my own initiative, I got into my car, switched on the engine, and drove towards Bosanka.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What time was it when you heard the radio news about what was going on in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour. I don't get any interpretation. I don't know whether something has happened to the system.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English channel? Can you hear the English interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can now. We did not hear.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said he heard it in a news bulletin broadcast over Radio Herceg-Novi. That was the answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately we're not getting the interpretation on channel 6 into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know what has gone on. If there could be a check made of what is happening. It is now functioning again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you respond to my question again, Mr. Novakovic. My question was: At what time did you hear the news about what was going on in Dubrovnik over the radio? What was the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, 1991, at 1500 hours, I listened to the local news bulletin, and the broadcaster in the news bulletin said that there was fighting at Srdj, near Dubrovnik, and that two men had been killed. And on my own initiative, I left the house, switched the engine of my jeep on that I hadn't returned, and, as fast as possible, drove to Bosanka.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So at 1500 hours on 6 December 1991, from what you heard over the radio news bulletin, there was combat action going on in Dubrovnik at that time? That was what you heard?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And where did you drive to from your home? What was the first place -- location you drove to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I drove straight from Herceg-Novi to Bosanka.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And how long did it take you to drive to Bosanka?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: About 35 to 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you said in examination-in-chief that when you drove to Bosanka, you drove via Brgat, Zarkovica, and then to Bosanka. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And as such, when you drove by Zarkovica, you would have noticed the combat activity that was being carried out on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. When I passed by Cavtat, at exactly the spot that there's the plaque saying Cavtat, you have a good vision all over the area and you can see the repeater at Srdj. And at that point in time, I saw three or four, let's say, or five to six, shells falling on the repeater at Srdj, and as there was a strong wind blowing from north to south, from the sea, I saw the wind carrying the smoke from the shells that fell, not from Zarkovica but from Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question to you was: When you passed Zarkovica, did you notice any combat activity or had it ceased by that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Everything had ceased by that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what time was it when you passed Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if it took me 45 minutes, I just spent three minutes -- three minutes before that I was at Zarkovica, because it takes three minutes from Zarkovica to Bosanka.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Why did you take that road? Is that the normal route that one would take going to Bosanka, or what was the reason for you to drive by Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have any reason to stop at Zarkovica, because Komarica, the man I was going to visit --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, my question to you was: Why did you take that particular road, that is, Brgat, Zarkovica, and Bosanka? What was the reason for you to take that route? Is that the usual route one would take going to Bosanka, or was there any special reason that you had for you to drive by Zarkovica? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: From Zarkovica to Bosanka, there are two routes. There's the asphalt road, which is the short route, and there is the hairpin bend road, which is not an asphalt road, which takes longer. So I took the shorter road.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you said the day after the event you went to the command post of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade. Where was that located?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was at Brgat.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How did you know this was the command post of the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not know that the command post was there, but in the vehicle there was Komarica Marko and Svetislav Rakovic, who brought me to their command, and it was only on that day that I actually learnt that their headquarters were there and that they weren't subordinated to the military naval sector but that they were attached to the second army of General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And who wasn't subordinated to the 9th Naval Sector by General Strugar? Who told you that? How did you learn that these persons you're speaking of were not subordinated to the 9th Naval Sector but to General Strugar? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I was saying, this unit of Rambo Kovacevic's, that unit was in a way on our territory, on our terrain. So I didn't know that they were subordinated to General Strugar. So that means when everything was over, and when we came to ask permission for these two soldiers to go to Subotica, that was when I came to realise that the unit of Marko Komarica, in actual fact, belonged, if I could put it that way, to the 2nd -- whatever you call it, to General Strugar, not the naval military sector. Because as an ordinary soldier I didn't go into those details, who belonged to whom. That wasn't what I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So what was it about going to Subotica that made you realise that the particular unit was within the command of the -- of General Strugar? What was it that made you realise it? Could you explain it better.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Now that I give it some thought, I can tell you that even at the time, I didn't actually realise -- or rather, towards the end I came to realise this they weren't actually under -- because captain of the warship Zec told Kovacevic, "You're going to have a longer holiday now." And when I left the building, I saw the reservists, from Herzegovina, who said, "We're not going to let Rambo be replaced," and all the other things they said. So later on I came to understand that Rambo's unit was not under the same command as I was, but that it was under the command of General Strugar. But I realised that only later. Because I couldn't have known that they were Strugar's men and not our men, that is to say, belonging to the military naval sector of Boka.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So what you're saying is their conduct and the manner they behaved at that stage made you realise that they were, to use your own term, words, Strugar's men and did not really belong to the military naval sector. That's what you felt?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked them where they were from, and they said some were from Trebinje, some were from Bileca. And then I realised, only then, from these ordinary soldiers, reservists, I realised that they weren't in fact linked to the military naval sector of Admiral Jokic, but that they were in fact up there. And I didn't know that General Strugar was their commander at all. All I knew was that they belonged to somebody else. So at the time, I didn't realise that Strugar was in fact their commander. I hadn't heard of Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you say "them," are you referring to members of the 3rd Battalion, 3rd Motorised Battalion of the 472nd Brigade? Is that what you're referring to when you say "them"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 3rd Battalion, commanded by Rambo Kovacevic, had regular soldiers as well as reserve soldiers. And from the regular soldiers on that day, I spoke to Komarica and Rakovic Svetislav. I never asked Komarica, "Who is your commander?" I just simply thought that those units from Herceg-Novi [as interpreted] and us were at the same level. We were not above them. I thought that we were all subordinated to some command from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the transcript, line 65 -- page 65, line 20, is should -- it says from Herceg-Novi, but it should actually state from Herzegovina. That's the correct term.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I be permitted to ask that again, Your Honour? My understanding was that it was Herceg-Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, could you just repeat what you just said. Did you say: I just simply thought that those units from Herceg-Novi and us were the same level, or did you say those units from Herzegovina and us were at the same level? Which of these did you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Units from Herzegovina, not from Herceg-Novi. There's no logic to them being just from Herceg-Novi. So units from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when -- you said Captain Zec said something to the effect of, "Young man, you have to go on a long vacation," or something to that effect, was it your understanding, or did it seem to you that the 9th Naval Sector was trying to have him removed and replaced? Is that what you understood, how you understood that statement to be?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I thought, even then, and I had confirmation, that Rambo Kovacevic and his unit was subordinated to the military naval sector, because the warship Captain Zec told him, "You will be going for a longer holiday." So that made me think that he was ours and not from the Herzegovina part.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But you changed your view about it, something that happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot change my position. I know that very well. Perhaps there was a mistranslation. You can repeat it and I will tell it to you again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. My question to you was: When Captain Zec asked -- indicated to him, "You have to go on a long holiday," did it seem to you that he was being removed or an attempt to remove him or replace him or how did you understand that statement to be?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I understood the statement to mean that he would have to, that in the opinion of captain of the warship Zec, he had made some mistakes and that he would be removed from the unit, that he would be punished, in a way. Even then, I thought that Rambo Kovacevic was subordinated to Zec and that Zec was subordinated to Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But having spoken to some other members of the 3rd Battalion, you realised that, to use your own language, they were Strugar's men, you said.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. When I saw the members of the reserves who had come to surround the command building and who were not allowing Rambo Kovacevic to be replaced, and when I understood that there was nobody there from Herceg-Novi or Boka, that all the people there were people from Herzegovina, then I understood that these were some other units. But even then, I didn't know that Strugar was commanding those units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So when did you know that Strugar was commanding the units? Was it on the 7th of December that you got to know? When did you find out? When did you realise this? You just said earlier on that you realised this.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I only understood that after I spoke with these members of the reserves, when I saw how resolute they were to defend him. Then I understood that things were not perhaps what I thought and that Rambo was not subordinated to the Boka naval military sector but to somebody else, to somebody from Herzegovina. And now I understand that he, his brigade, was part -- or the 3rd Brigade was part of the units commanded by Strugar. So I only understood that now. Well, when there were -- there was talk about the trial, about two years ago, or perhaps on some programmes on television, that's when I really understood it, and now I'm just trying to help you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. And if I understand you well, what you're saying is you felt that there was some form of resistance amongst the reservists belonging to the 3rd Battalion towards the officers of the naval sector, and therefore -- and there was some evidence that indicated they had authority from another higher command. Is that how you understood it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't receive their orders from any command, but on their own initiative they wished to defend their commander Kovacevic, and they opposed the decision of the Boka Military Naval Sector. Admiral Jokic and warship Captain Zec. And with their presence, by the fact that they surrounded the building, they prevented him from being replaced. So that Rambo Kovacevic remained the commander of that unit. They succeeded in their objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Moving on, Mr. Novakovic. You said that you found out that the 3rd Battalion troops had arrived at the top of Srdj when the mortars -- or when fire was opened on them from the city of Dubrovnik. And when I say "city," I'm talking about the wider area of Dubrovnik and not the Old Town. What time -- did you find out what time it was when those units had reached the top of Srdj?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. They set out early in the morning and they arrived sometime during the day. I don't know exactly what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to what time the two members were killed? You said you found out that they had arrived at the top and then there was fire at them from Dubrovnik and two members were killed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They said over Radio Herceg-Novi that there were two dead, but when I got to Bosanka, I heard, and later I saw them at the morgue, that there were five dead. And most of them were killed by mortar shells which came from the direction of Dubrovnik. Because those who were at the repeater were not able to defend the repeater any more. They asked for assistance from Dubrovnik, and these people were fired at from certain spots in Dubrovnik, the people of Rambo Kovacevic, and five of them were killed. In order to protect his soldiers, he fired at Dubrovnik, and what happened, happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you say "repeater," what you mean is the Croatian forces at the facility in Srdj sought assistance from their positions in the wider area of Dubrovnik, and they opened fire on those JNA soldiers who had managed to approach Srdj? That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: They were not in the general sector of Dubrovnik. We were in the general sector of Dubrovnik. They were in Dubrovnik and they fired from certain points. I remember that Rakovic and Komarica told me from which spots, but I forgot what they were. It was next to certain hotels. So these men were shot at from Dubrovnik, and that's how they were killed. I know that the fire came from the central area of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you say "central area," if I give you certain names, such as Babin Kuk, Lapad, Dubravka, are those the areas you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps not Dubravka, but Lapad, perhaps Babin Kuk. There's the Medarevo hospital there, and there were mortars behind the hospital. There were positions. I don't know whether this was the case in this operation, but I know that when I was in the Dubrovnik front, mortars were positioned exactly behind the Medarevo clinic, maternity clinic, and I don't know whether these were neutralised or not. But I do remember that their weapons were positioned behind Medarevo in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And Medarevo is outside the Old Town, towards the west of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you were informed about -- at least, you said that you learnt that on the 5th there had been a meeting where the plan to attack Srdj was approved. I'm sorry. I think what you said was Captain Zec had asked certain officers to volunteer, or certain soldiers to volunteer to attack Srdj on the 6th. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Komarica Marko and Svetislav Rakovic told me that in my house when I brought them from the Meljine hospital to spend the night at my house so that I could take them where I was taking them in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, who had been present at this meeting where Captain Zec had asked them to volunteer? Were there other soldiers apart from these two persons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Bodiroga was there for sure, and Mesaros, and the rest I didn't know. I've never seen them before. I only know what these two men told me, that the captain of the warship Zec asked that unit that was assembled there who was brave enough to drive those grannies from Srdj. And they told me that there was a silence for a couple of seconds, and Bodiroga volunteered first, and when he did that, then his section, Komarica, Rakovic, Mesaros all volunteered. So that was the section. One of the squads. Because I think there were attacks from several points. I only know about this one. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon for that interruption. Mr. Novakovic, the people that you spoke of who were killed in the November operation where you had to evacuate the casualties, to which command or to which units did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This was the Herceg-Novi Territorial Defence. Those who were killed were from the Herceg-Novi TO. And as they were being pulled out, Baja Bajkovic from Bar was killed, as well as Baja Radovic from Niksic. These were two men who were not from the Herceg-Novi TO but they were killed while they were pulling out our men. Also three of our men were killed and maybe seven, eight, to ten other men were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And they were wounded in the course of conducting certain operations in the time period 8 November to 13th November, isn't it? They were killed in the course of combat activity; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The specials unit from Herceg-Novi were breaking through in the Dubac-Brgat sector, and in the afternoon they came to Brgat and they went to one house, and Colonel Jovanovic, called Kurd, came to them and suggested that they go on reconnaissance with him, and they did that. But in fact, he brought them into direct combat on the 8th of November in Bosanka.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that the 3rd Battalion participated in the operations conducted in November? Do you know that in the combat operations conducted by the JNA, the 3rd Battalion, the 3rd Motorised Brigade of the 472nd Motorised Brigade also participated? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. As I said, out of that whole battalion, I only knew Marko Komarica. I wasn't -- I didn't ask him which unit he was in. I just accepted him as a young soldier who had taken part in rescuing some of my friends from Herceg-Novi. Some people from Herceg-Novi did not have the courage to pull out the dead and the wounded, and this Marko Komarica was brave enough to do that. So I never really asked him about any of his military tasks and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But he was involved in that even evacuation. This person was present in the course of the operations; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was there during the operation, but I was not. So simply, I'm a radio mechanic, and my job is completely different. So other than my Herceg-Novi TO, I wasn't really paying much attention about which units were there, who belonged to what. I would be distributing the batteries to the radio stations, and I really didn't have too much information about who was doing what.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I don't mean to be rude, but would you please confine your response to my questions. My question is: The fact that your friend who belonged to the 3rd Battalion was involved in the combat operations should indicate to you, as a person with a military background, that the 3rd Battalion was in fact involved in the naval operations; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I only know for sure that the 3rd Battalion participated in the attack on the 6th of December on Srdj. As far as the Bosanka attack is concerned, I didn't even know that attack would take place. I had no idea who was attacking, why it was being attacked. And even that day, I had asked the commander to let me go home so I can have a shower and so on. So when I got home, I received a phone call informing me that there were wounded and killed, and that is when I went to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do you know that the casualties, those wounded and killed, was due to firing from the Croatian positions in areas such as Lapad, Babin Kuk, you know, what we discussed earlier on? Was it from the same positions that they were fired at?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Bosanka was full of Croat soldiers at the time. They were fired at from Bosanka, and perhaps from some other locations that I don't know about. I didn't take part in those battles.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, you mentioned one Colonel Jovanovic. Do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know we're talking about Colonel Jovanovic, and his nickname was Kurd. I know that there were three Jovanovics. I know he came from somewhere outside the area, because out of these other two, I know one, Tomislav Jovanovic, he's a colonel from some other army branch dealing with road construction. I know him personally. I even had a small conflict with him at Brgat, so I know exactly who we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And whom did you have a conflict with? Was it with Colonel Tomislav Jovanovic or the other colonel that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I just had a conflict with Colonel Jovanovic, nicknamed Kurd, not with Tomislav Jovanovic. And there was yet a third Jovanovic. And also, Tomislav Jovanovic is here in The Hague with me, and I often referred to this other Jovanovic. I saw there were two. And he says no, there were three. So there were three Jovanovics.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So did you discuss or did you have opportunity to speak with Colonel Tomislav Jovanovic here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We're in the same hotel. I talked to him and I mentioned this Colonel Jovanovic to him. Because he was a special kind of man.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you also discuss or speak to -- I think you said Colonel Djurasic, is also present at the moment in The Hague. Did you also speak to him? Can you speak up a little, Mr. Novakovic? I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Not Djurisic. Djurasic. He's in the same hotel where I am here in The Hague. And during this week, he will most probably appear here before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yeah. My question to you was: Did you also speak with him about these issues? Did you have the opportunity to talk to him while here in The Hague at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. No. We didn't discuss that subject. Because we have nothing to discuss with regard to these subjects. He did a different thing. He was in Grude and I don't know where. And I went my own way. So I really don't know Gojko Djurasic. We just socialised at the hotel, talked about other things. We talked about the Dubrovnik theatre of war least of all because we have nothing in common there. We were not in the same operation at any point in time. So there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, you said you went home on 2nd or 3rd December, but were you at any stage informed that on the 5th there had been some negotiations to conclude a comprehensive cease-fire on the 6th? Were you ever informed of that at any stage, either before or after the 6th December incident?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I never heard of that. This is the first time I hear about it from you, that there was such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So were you anticipating being -- were you expected to go back to the front to get involved in combat activity when you went back home on the 2nd or 3rd?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: We did not expect either. We were simply sent back home, and we were waiting to see what the higher command would decide. The higher command decided that we should return our things and that we should go, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you testified that Colonel Kovacevic, Colonel Gavro Kovacevic, had informed one of your friends that there was a mortar firing from the Old Town on a truck. This you heard from a friend you spoke to after the incident in November?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That night, when I returned for a second time from Brgat to Zarkovica so that we could try to go towards Bosanka to find Savo Vidakovic and to try to find other people who were wounded or dead --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may interrupt. My question to you is: Your friend, Gaso Mijatovic - and pardon me for mispronouncing that name - informed you that Colonel Kovacevic said something to the effect that there was a mortar firing from a truck from the Old Town, and this was in November. My question to you is: You heard this from a friend Gaso Mijatovic; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what Gaso Mijatovic told me. He heard that from conversations when he went up to Zarkovica to find out what was going on so that he could find Vojica Pejovic, who was dead. Then Gavro Kovacevic said to him --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt. We are under time constraint. And how did Gaso Mijatovic find this out? Who told this to Gaso Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Gavro Kovacevic said that to Gaso. He was there wearing a helmet and in a very serious situation, because all day he was under mortar fire from the Old Town, and he said, "I was even targeted by a mortar called Charlie from Dubrovnik mounted on this little truck," and this mortar was firing at him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this was told to you by Gaso Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this was in November, in the course of the November operation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, where did Gaso Mijatovic say that Colonel Kovacevic was at the time he spoke with Colonel Kovacevic? Where was Colonel Kovacevic at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kovacevic was at Zarkovica, in his command house, and then Gaso Mijatovic entered that house to ask him what the situation was like at Bosanka, where his friend Vojica Pejovic was. He gave him all these answers correctly. And when he asked him where his friend was, then he turned his back to him and then Gaso Mijatovic walked out and then -- I told you what happened then. I mentioned that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So this statement of Colonel Kovacevic was in the spirit of sending Gaso Mijatovic, was asking him for a favour, asking Colonel Kovacevic to help withdraw his friend from difficulty, when he asked him that, Colonel Kovacevic said, "I can't help this, but in fact I myself am under fire from the Old Town." It was in a sense of dismissing Gaso Mijatovic that he said this; is that correct? Do I take that as a yes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it could be put that way, somehow.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And from Zarkovica, there is an unobstructed view into the Old Town; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Which also goes to indicate that obviously from the Old Town, there is a view into Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And at this time when Gaso Mijatovic spoke to Colonel Kovacevic, were they standing on Zarkovica itself, in clear view of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In this house in Zarkovica. They cannot be seen. The entrance is from the eastern side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So did your friend Gaso Mijatovic tell you that while he was there at Zarkovica, this so-called mortar from the vehicle Charlie fired at Zarkovica, or was it the case that he merely conveyed to you what Colonel Kovacevic said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: He just told me what Colonel Kovacevic had said to him, that throughout the day, on several occasions, he was exposed to mortar fire from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, have you yourself seen the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that the only place in the Old Town where a truck could move around is the Stradun? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So if there was in fact a vehicle on Stradun, it would be in clear view of Zarkovica, the position at Zarkovica, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Stradun is long. It's hard for me to recall all of this, but there must be points on Stradun, and in other streets, where it could be tucked in and where it could not be seen from Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, the streets, the other streets, are little alleys on other side of Stradun, isn't it? You have Stradun going from east to west across the Old Town, and on either side, going towards north to south, you have little alleys in behind very high walls. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the alleys on the side facing Srdj consist of steps. There are steps going up those alleys, alleyways; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are streets with steps, and there are streets with cobblestones, or stone pavement, whatever the word may be.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The streets with the cobblestones are to the south of the Stradun, while the streets with the steps are to the north of the Stradun; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So clearly, it's needless to say that it would be impossible to have a truck in any one of those streets on the northern side, since they consist of steps. You agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the little alleyways on the south to the Stradun are extremely narrow. Wouldn't it be -- isn't it logical to contemplate a truck going in any one of those narrow alleyways?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not a question of logical or illogical. I wasn't watching that, you see. Because that day, when I was between Zarkovica and Bosanka, when this killing took place at 3.00 on the 6th, nobody was operating then. I just saw plumes of smoke coming from a few different places in Dubrovnik, but that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. I didn't suggest that you saw this. My point was that since you have some background knowledge of the area, Dubrovnik and the Old Town, my question was: Wouldn't you agree with me if I put it to you that it would be logical to have a truck going down any one of those alleyways, due to the width of those streets. The transcript reads would be illogical but it should be logical -- illogical.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I'm not a military expert. Military experts should be asked whether there are localities in the Old Town where such a vehicle could move and fire at Zarkovica and other places. I personally think that there are such places, because it is a well-known thing how a mortar shell travels. So that can be explained very nicely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, in your -- in the period that you served in the Dubrovnik operation, did you ever receive any orders or instructions with regard to the protected status of the Old Town? Were you ever told that the Old Town was a protected site and it should not be fired upon?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody told me that, but that goes without saying. Whenever I was nearby, I did not see, ever, any attack by our artillery against Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. My question to you was not that. I'm sure that you personally are aware that it's a protected site. But my question was: Did you receive any orders or instructions from your higher command, saying: Do not fire on the Old Town? Or that the Old Town is a protected site, so you should not fire upon it? Did you receive any orders to such effect?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm an ordinary soldier. Nobody had any need to issue me that kind of order. I'm a mechanic. I do my own job.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you just indicate as to what the distance between the Old Town and Zarkovica is.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is it possible from Zarkovica to see a vehicle and also identify what type of weapon is placed on the vehicle? My question is: Is it possible from Zarkovica to see a vehicle in -- which is supposed to be located in the Old Town? And also identify the type of weapon that's on the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what? From Zarkovica, that can be seen. Probably even with the naked eye. But military people have binoculars and different other equipment with which they can establish exactly what is where.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, when did -- did you learn that the Old Town was shelled in the course of the 6 December attack? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I learnt that when I came at 1540 hours, for instance, when I came from Zarkovica to Bosanka. From Zarkovica I saw that Dubrovnik had suffered some damage because I saw plumes of smoke arising from some localities in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm asking specifically with regard to the Old Town. Did you see smoke coming from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw smoke from the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you inquire from your colleagues in the 3rd Battalion as to what had happened, whether they fired on the Old Town? Did you have any such conversation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have that kind of conversation. I just came to see what was going on with Komarica, whether he was dead or alive, whether he was wounded or not. That was the only thing I was interested in. No one made any comments. It was just obvious that something had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do you know that in fact it was units of the 3rd Battalion that shelled the Old Town on 6 December?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was: In talking to Rakovic and Komarica, I understood that when their five comrades were killed, fighting for the peak, the repeater at Srdj, and when they reported it to the command that they had five men killed, then they tried to shoot at the points from which they were targeted when their four fellow soldiers were killed. And that's the information I got from Komarica.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did Komarica tell you that they shelled the Old Town on 6 December or they attacked the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. Komarica didn't tell me that they had attacked the Old Town because Komarica, or rather his detachment had the assignment of taking control of the repeater at Srdj and that was Bodiroga's group from Trebinje, and they volunteered and that was their assignment to take the repeater at Srdj. He had nothing to do with Dubrovnik that day actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did he tell you that other units of the 3rd Battalion shelled the Old Town? Not his unit perhaps but other units of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. We didn't discuss that. They just told me how their five fellow soldiers were killed and Rakovic told me that Komarica was in a very difficult situation on several occasions, and it seemed that they were targeting him because whenever he moved, a shell would fall in the spot he had previously been. So he did all -- it was by chance that he came out alive, being targeted that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, do you know as to whether Captain Kovacevic was present at the meeting on 5th December, when Captain Zec had asked your friends to volunteer? Was Captain Kovacevic of the 3rd Battalion present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that specific detail. I know that those guys were present and that captain of the warship Zec was present. Now, whether Kovacevic was there or not, I can't say. It would be logical that he was, but I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what time was it when you heard from your friend Komarica that five soldiers were killed on Srdj? At what time had they been killed in the course of the attack on 6 December?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The attack began early in the morning, and they were killed when I arrived at 1540 hours. Everything was over by that time. They were all killed and wounded and sent to hospital. So when I arrived at Bosanka, there wasn't a single person there, either killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. My question is: Do you know at what time they were killed or wounded on Srdj, these five people? Do you know? Did your friend Komarica tell you at what time they were killed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't specific about the time. All he said was that when they reached the top where the repeater at Srdj was, that this was a plateau and that the shelling was terrible and that the wind was very strong that day. So they tried to do what they could, but they couldn't actually do anything, so they returned, went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know that after this incident Captain Kovacevic of the 3rd Battalion was promoted? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How would you describe the discipline in the units with which you worked and in your unit? Was there a lot of looting, arson, drinking, unauthorised opening of fire by individual soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In my unit, up until the 8th of November, until our fellow soldiers were killed, we had a high level of discipline. There were no great problems. Perhaps drinking a little bit of alcohol, because Konavle is well known for its brandy and wine. So there was brandy and wine. People did drink. But the command was in control of the situation and the terrain and there were no serious problems. Now, after the 8th, the problems started, because the soldiers no longer had -- could place their trust and confidence in their officers. So the protest Kumbor took place and the situation was somewhat different at the end of it all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And how would you describe the military police units that you may have observed in the course of the Dubrovnik operation? Did it seem to you that they were conducting their investigations, charging people, or did you see any form of shortcomings in the -- amongst the military units? I'm talking about -- I'm sorry - military police units.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as to the military police, I didn't come across them much, so I really can't say. I can't tell you anything about that. Perhaps I came across them once or twice. But they were mostly people working in the field rather than the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Haven't you seen military police units checking ID cards and carrying out guard duty at checkpoints on the roads? You have seen military police units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: At Debeli Brijeg, which is the border between Herceg-Novi and Dubrovnik, or rather, Croatia and Montenegro. That's where the military police was. And every -- all the vehicles were searched, going out and coming in, on both sides. And there was a checkpoint somewhere along there, I think by Cavtat, or the airport at Cilipi. I'm not quite sure, because a lot of time has gone by. There was a checkpoint. But as to the checkpoint at the border crossing, that was a very strict checkpoint, whereas the others weren't as strict.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know how many reservists were involved in the protests or demonstrations in front of Kumbor that you spoke of, you know, where -- after the November operations, they protested in front of the 9th VPS command post or headquarters in Kumbor. And do you know how many reservists were involved?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know how many reservists were there. I wasn't there, actually. I was busy pulling out the dead below the repeater at Srdj. So I really don't know. All I know is that it took place, it happened, but I don't know how many of them there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do you know, in fact, that the demonstration was an attempt calling upon the 9th VPS command to pursue the war energetically? Wasn't that the reason for the protest? In fact, they were protesting that the 9th VPS did not come through as pursuing the war more energetically, and you in fact said that they considered the 9th VPS to be weak or something; you used some word to such effect?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Quite simply, they were angry because their fellow soldiers were killed at Bosanka and that they hadn't been taken care of quickly enough. So that was the reason. But I wasn't actually there myself, so I can't really make a judgement which would be 100 per cent correct. But that's how it was, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the time, namely, we just have a minute left, may I be allowed to continue tomorrow, but for just 15 minutes or so, just briefly, not more than that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Rodic. We will adjourn now for the evening. Mr. Novakovic, if you would be kind enough to return tomorrow morning. The hearing will continue at 9.00 in the morning. Thank you.
